title: Nervous Control, Muscles and Homeostasis
seo_title: Year 13 A Level Biology: Response and Homeostasis Worksheets
standard_code: A level Biology: Organisms respond to changes in their environments
standard_text: Plant growth factors and tropisms, taxes and kineses, reflexes, receptors, control of heart rate, nerve impulses and synapses, skeletal muscle contraction, and homeostasis: control of blood glucose and of blood water potential by the kidney.
meta_desc: Free Year 13 A level biology worksheets on response and homeostasis: action potentials, synapses, muscle contraction, insulin and glucagon, the kidney, ADH and tropisms. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Speed = distance ÷ time (mm per ms = m s⁻¹).
body_html:
How to think about it

An action potential happens when voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open (depolarisation) and then K⁺ channels open (repolarisation). Myelin gives saltatory conduction. At synapses, Ca²⁺ triggers release of neurotransmitter, which diffuses across the cleft. In muscle, Ca²⁺ exposes binding sites on actin and ATP drives the myosin heads.

Insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon raises it. In the kidney, ultrafiltration happens at the glomerulus, glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, and ADH makes the collecting duct more permeable to water.

Example

50 mm in 2.0 ms. Speed?

50 mm ÷ 2.0 ms

Answer: 25 m s⁻¹

Example

Refractory period 2 ms. Maximum frequency?

1 ÷ 0.002 s

Answer: 500 Hz

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting that 1 mm/ms = 1 m/s.
  • Saying bigger stimuli give bigger action potentials.
  • Mixing up insulin and glucagon.

faq.a: In myelinated axons the impulse jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next, so it travels faster.
It makes the walls of the collecting duct more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed and urine is more concentrated.
